mcqs.question: Why is client-side hiding of a UI element (e.g. hiding an admin button when no token is present) never sufficient authentication?
options: The client can be tampered with, so any check performed only there can't be trusted as proof of identity
Client-side checks are always slower than server-side checks
Browsers block JavaScript from reading tokens entirely
It only works for mobile apps, not web browsers
mcqs.explanation: A client is under the user's control, so any authentication logic living only there can be bypassed or spoofed — it's a UX convenience, not a security boundary. Speed isn't the issue, browsers don't block token reads, and the limitation applies to mobile apps just as much as browsers.

mcqs.question: A security team needs the ability to instantly kill a specific user's login the moment a compromise is detected. Which auth model makes that easiest to guarantee?
options: A signed JWT with a 24-hour expiry and no blocklist
Session-based auth with a central session store
A signed JWT with a 30-day expiry
Any stateless token scheme, since they scale better
mcqs.explanation: Session-based auth stores the source of truth server-side, so deleting one row instantly invalidates the session everywhere. A long-lived stateless JWT stays valid until it expires regardless of what the server wants, unless you add a blocklist — which reintroduces the shared-state lookup tokens were meant to avoid. Scaling better doesn't help if revocation is the actual requirement.

mcqs.question: What does mTLS between two internal services actually prove?
options: That the end user is authorized to perform the action being requested
That the request has been rate-limited correctly
Which service is making the call, independent of any user context
That the data in transit has never been read by a third party
mcqs.explanation: mTLS establishes service identity — cryptographic proof of which service is on the other end of the connection — but says nothing about which end user's request triggered it or whether that user is authorized. That's why systems combine mTLS with a forwarded, scoped user claim when downstream permission checks are also needed.

mcqs.question: A team splits a monolith into ten services but has every new service query the monolith's original session table directly to check who's logged in. What's the main design problem with this?
options: Session tables can't store more than one active session per user
It's technically impossible — services in different processes can't share a database table
It will always be slower than token-based auth in every scenario
Every service now has a hard runtime dependency on shared internal state, making that table a single point of contention and coupling every service to the monolith's schema
mcqs.explanation: The split should extend to identity, not stop at business logic — otherwise every new service inherits a fragile, shared dependency on internal state it doesn't own. It's entirely possible technically (multiple services can query one table), and the problem isn't inherent speed, it's the coupling and single point of failure.

mcqs.question: A user logged in 6 hours ago and is now trying to change their payout bank account. Why might the system reject this with a step-up challenge even though the session is still valid?
options: Sessions are only ever valid for exactly one hour, so this session has technically expired
The sensitive action requires fresher or stronger authentication proof than the general login already provided
Payout changes always require a completely new account to be created
This is a bug — a valid session should authorize any action without restriction
mcqs.explanation: Step-up auth exists precisely because a general login and a sensitive action don't warrant the same trust level — the action needs a recency/strength check (like recent MFA) independent of whether the session itself is still valid. Session lifetime isn't necessarily one hour, no new account is needed, and treating every action as equally trusted by a stale login is the exact gap step-up auth closes.
